The cleanest solution seems to be letting the bird move inward as the sky gets narrower rather than clamping the sky width itself, which keeps the runway consistent without visual padding.

Actually, I can simplify this entirely by dropping the clamp altogether—the panel has a hard floor at 360 anyway, so there's no risk of it collapsing to nothing. The game will just be slightly harder at narrow widths and easier at wide ones, which is honest and matches how other side-scrollers behave across viewports. I'm working through the layout dimensions for the game field. With a default width of 480 pixels minus padding, the field is about 448 wide, and based on the screenshot proportions, roughly 950 pixels tall, giving me an aspect ratio around 0.47. This breaks down to about 170 pixels for the sky, 54 for the bird position, and 116 for the runway, which works out to a reasonable 1.2 second flight time. At the narrowest viewport of 360 pixels, the proportions scale down to 328 wide with adjusted sky and runway heights, bringing the flight time down to about 0.88 seconds.

The challenge is that at narrow widths, the bird needs enough runway ahead to make the game playable—roughly 115 units at the current speed to maintain that 1.2 second window. But a tall narrow panel doesn't show much sky ahead, so I'm considering anchoring the sky width at a fixed 240 pixels instead and letting the height float based on the aspect ratio. This would give me a taller sky in portrait orientations, making the flap mechanic feel more proportional to the screen and spreading the pipe gaps over a larger vertical range.

The tradeoff is that anchoring height keeps the game feel consistent across all panel sizes—the bird's flap height, gap size, and bird scale all stay the same relative to the screen—while anchoring width would make narrow panels require more flapping to cross the same visual distance. I think keeping the feel consistent matters more than reaction time varying slightly, so I'm leaning toward sticking with the height anchor and accepting that narrow panels are tighter. But 0.88 seconds of runway at the narrowest is pretty rough, so I'm exploring a compromise: capping how far right the bird can spawn in wider panels to prevent them from becoming trivially easy, while ensuring narrow panels always have a minimum runway.

Actually, I'm overthinking this. The honest framing is that the sky is as wide as the field and the bird stands 30% in from the left. A 360px panel is the narrowest anyone can make it, and yes, the game gets harder there—just like any side-scroller is harder on a narrow screen. Real Flappy Bird on a phone gives about 1.2 seconds of runway, and we're hitting 0.9 seconds at the extreme and 1.2 seconds at the default, which is fine.

Wait, there's a cleaner approach I keep skirting around: what if pipe spacing and speed are both defined in world units, and the world itself...

Actually, no. I need to stop and ship the simple rule. The sky width scales with the aspect ratio, the bird sits at 30% of the width, no clamping. But there's one edge case I should guard against: if the field ever becomes 1 pixel wide, the sky collapses to nearly zero and pipes spawn at 40 while the bird is at 0, which means instant death. The panel has a minimum of 360 pixels though, and the field is measured properly, so a zero-size field should fall back to the default sky width via the height check.

When the panel closes with a CSS transition, the outer div shrinks but the inner content stays fixed and gets clipped—the game field doesn't actually resize, so that's safe. And switching tabs unmounts the whole GameView anyway. Still, a minimum floor on the sky width is cheap protection against any weird measurement edge cases, so I'll keep that in place.

I'll set NARROWEST to 120—at the narrowest real panel width of 328, the sky calculates to 124, so the floor never actually triggers in practice. If it somehow did engage on a degenerate case, the image would just clip at the right edge, which is fine. No letterboxing needed.

The mask region actually extends much further right to x=812, but Chromium clips the rendered layer to the viewport boundary at 652—exactly where the line appears. When masked content gets drawn into a transparency layer and sampled at that boundary, you get artifacts from the compositing process trying to sample just outside the clipped region.

The solution is simple: keep the painted rectangles (the sky, flash, and color rects) from extending all the way to the viewport edge. Instead of letting them reach x=812 and getting hard-clipped at 652, I should constrain them to stay within the visible bounds.

It's positioned far to the left with a negative cx value, but it's still rendering a full-height column somehow, even though it should be masked and invisible at opacity 0. The ellipse has a warm reddish-grey fill that matches the line I'm seeing.

The culprit is the radial gradient with default `gradientUnits="objectBoundingBox"` combined with the CSS transform. When the ellipse gets its own composited tile due to the active transform, the gradient's tile mode clamps to the last color stop (white), which bleeds beyond the gradient's bounds and shows up at the viewport edge.

But wait — the observed color is warm (53,44,31), not white. That's the mesh's orange blob showing through at low opacity. So the leak isn't the sweep itself; it's the masked group's content escaping because the sweep's animation extends the group's bounds far to the right with `translateX(880px)`, forcing a larger invalidation rect that gets clipped at the viewport edge.

I'm considering fixes: either constrain the sweep to prevent the seam, or add a transparent gutter inside the viewport so the clip edge sits on empty space. But the mesh spans the whole field, so bounding the rects won't help — the leak column is right at the viewport clip boundary.

Actually, I should test whether the leak is really the clip edge or the last column of the mask bitmap itself. If I widen the SVG and the line stays at 644 instead of moving with the viewport, that tells me something different.

The practical solution is to remove the sweep's massive translate since the sweep is the light effect that runs across the discs as the last one lands — it's intentional design, but it's what's causing the leak.

I can't just delete it, so I need to redraw it differently. One approach is to animate the gradient itself rather than translating the ellipse, though SVG gradient stops aren't easy to animate with CSS. Another option is to keep the ellipse but constrain its travel to just cross the mark area, starting off-screen and ending within bounds.

I could also wrap the sweep in its own group with a clip-path matching the visible box, which would prevent the layer from extending past the viewport—though the clipping edge itself might introduce antialiasing artifacts. Or I could paint the sweep as a stationary rect filled with an animated gradient, where the gradient's transform moves instead of the element itself. I'm wondering if the leak column is positioned at the viewport edge or at a fixed coordinate in user space—that's the key to solving this. Let me test by expanding the room size and seeing whether the column stays a fixed distance from the SVG's right edge or moves with it, which would tell me if it's viewport-relative or coordinate-relative.

If enlarging the room just pushes the clip boundary further out while the paint still extends all the way across, the seam will keep leaking the mesh color. The real fix is to bound all the painted rectangles to a paint boundary that only covers where the discs can actually reach, then keep the viewport larger than that boundary so there's nothing to leak at the clip edge. The sweep animation reaches out to 880 though, which extends past where I'd want to constrain the paint, so I need to figure out how to handle that.

Actually, looking closer — the seam color during the 0–120ms window when the sweep is fully transparent must be coming from the mesh itself, not the sweep. So if I limit the mesh and currentColor rectangles to stop at 644 horizontally and keep the viewport at 692, the seam at the clip boundary would have no painted content to leak. Actually, there's a potentially better approach: what if the sweep animation doesn't render at all until it's needed, rather than existing as a huge travelling ellipse the whole time? The seam only shows during the backwards fill phase anyway.

Wait, but the element has to stay in the DOM since CrewLogo restarts animations by replaying them. Looking more closely at the timing, the seam appears at 0–120ms (backwards fill, translateX(0), opacity 0) and vanishes once the animation actually runs at 140–180ms. At rest (900ms, forwards fill), there's no seam either. So it's specifically when the sweep is positioned at translateX(0) with opacity 0 that the artifact appears—the ellipse's right edge sits exactly at x=0, which is the left boundary of the mark, not the right.

I'm wondering if this is related to how Chromium handles the radial gradient's tiling behavior. The sweep ellipse uses a radial gradient with objectBoundingBox units, where the gradient goes from white at 0.95 to transparent at 0. The ellipse's bounding box spans from -192 to 0, which actually falls outside the mask region (which is -180 to 812), so that might be contributing to the artifact.

Let me run some targeted experiments to isolate the cause. First, I'll try increasing the ROOM value to see if the seam moves with the viewport edge, then test removing the transform from the keyframe, and finally try reducing the BLEED value to see if any of these changes eliminate the seam.

Actually, thinking through E3 more carefully: with BLEED at 180, the field becomes enormous relative to the visible area—roughly 13 times wider than what's actually shown. When Chromium rasterizes the mask into a bitmap, it may scale down the rasterization for such a large region, and combined with the sweep extending even further, this could create a resampling artifact right at the clipped edge where the mask boundary is.

The real question is how much bleed is actually necessary. Looking at the paint requirements: the discs travel across a certain range at different scales, and there's vertical overshoot to account for. A much smaller bleed—around 16 units per direction—should be sufficient to cover all the movement without creating such an enormous offscreen buffer that triggers downsampling.

Setting BLEED to 24 would shrink the field to nearly the viewBox size, which is much more reasonable. The sweep element itself still travels far, but since it's a single element and fades to invisible opacity partway through, the visible portion never actually extends past a certain point. I can optimize the sweep's travel distance to match where it becomes invisible rather than letting it run all the way across.

I'm looking at how `saved-session.ts` generates the `code` field and whether git sync and the store can be decoupled. The architecture requires a git repo upfront since `startHost` validates this, and the store always lives in `.crew` at the repo root. Git sync runs automatically every 5 seconds in both host and join modes, committing the entire working tree while excluding `.crew` from the status reporting through `PROJECT_PATHS`.

Jamel's core insight is that these three concerns should be independent: where crew data persists (repo `.crew` folder versus app data directory keyed by project), whether git sync runs automatically, and whether the session is joinable by others. His Discord analogy reframes this—the repo itself becomes the server, so instead of choosing host or join upfront, you simply open a project and the session exists; joining becomes an optional feature you enable.

The current design forces all three together: pick host or join, require a git repo, auto-start sync, write everything to the repo. This makes local-only workflows impossible. A better approach would be to decouple these decisions so opening any folder creates a session with a persistent location for crew data, independent of whether git sync is active or whether others can join.

The implementation is straightforward: `Store` takes a root path parameter instead of hardcoding `.crew` inside the repo. Two options emerge—either `<repo>/.crew` for shared, committed crew workflows, or `~/Library/Application Support/Crew/projects/<hash>/` for private local work. Everything downstream (chat, docs, designs, attachments) follows automatically since they all live under that root. The tricky part is that if docs and boards live outside the repo, agents can't access them by file path—but since agents already read through the session and docs are served that way, it mostly works out.

For git syncing, I'd gate `GitSync.start()` so it only runs when enabled. When off, `git` becomes null and the UI controls quiet down, leaving explicit Pull/Push buttons for manual control. The `onBeforeRun` hook that calls `git.syncNow()` needs to become a no-op in that case.

For network access, the server currently binds to `0.0.0.0:2739` and generates a LAN link, but for solo work it should bind to `127.0.0.1` instead with no shareable link. Opening it up should be a toggle that controls which address the server listens on.

The model shifts to always hosting: you open a folder and Crew serves it locally, everything works out of the box. "Invite" becomes a button that opens the port and copies a link, while "Join" is the separate path on the home screen for accepting someone else's link. For git specifically, the repo acts as the server when it has a reachable remote and sync is enabled—without sync, a session is still joinable over LAN, just without code syncing.

For the constraint about not being able to write anything to the folder, the private root lives outside the repo and gets keyed by the folder's absolute path or a hash of it. Moving the folder orphans the history, but you could recover it from a recent projects list, or better yet, key by the repo's initial commit hash if it's a git repo—that survives moves and stays stable.

Without git at all, there's no reason to block Crew from working in local mode since files, terminal, and agents all function fine in a plain folder. The repo controls just become inactive, so I should drop that hard requirement and make it a folder property instead.

For the UI, I'm thinking of a Discord-like model: the home screen shows your recent projects plus options to open a folder or paste an invite, with no host/join toggle. Opening a project takes you straight in with an active session, and the top bar has a single control showing how the project is shared—closed by default with nothing committed or reachable.

On the sharing question, I'm realizing the history location can't be moved cheaply once it exists. Toggling between local and shared would require migrating `.crew` in and out of the repo each time, which is expensive and problematic. So instead, I should ask once when opening the folder: "Keep this project's crew in the folder?" That decision sticks and determines whether history lives locally or in the repo.

What's interesting is that multiplayer doesn't actually require git at all. The WebSocket server already broadcasts events and sends snapshots on connect, so a LAN session works for chat, agents, docs, and boards even without sync. Git sync is really just for pooling code and preserving history if the host goes offline. A work session where nothing gets committed can still have a coworker join over LAN.

Now I'm checking whether the joiner actually depends on git for anything essential. The joiner auto-pulls the repo while connected, and attachments come over HTTP from the host, docs and boards over WebSocket. So git only handles code movement. I should verify the chat history comes through the WebSocket snapshot, and also check what happens if there's no git repo at all—whether the system degrades gracefully or crashes.

The tradeoff with private history is real: docs become inaccessible to agents, boards don't sync to the repo, attachments stay local, and nothing transfers if you hand the project to someone else. For solo work that's probably fine. On the link sharing side, `crew://host:port/code` only works on LAN, so for broader access you'd need something like Tailscale or a rendezvous server. For the history key itself, I can use the genesis commit hash from `git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD`, falling back to a hash of the real path for non-git folders, with a note that multiple root commits just take the first one sorted.

There's an elegant solution hiding here: if the repo has a remote, the host can write its current link into a ref or file and joiners read it, making discovery automatic without needing a server. That turns the repo itself into the rendezvous point. But that requires git, which work forbids, so for work it's LAN or Tailscale only—which is fine since the whole point there is solo anyway.

Looked through `src/main/session.ts`, `src/server/store.ts`, `src/server/git.ts` and the Home screen. Here is what I think is going on and what I'd do.

## The problem is three things welded into one choice

Right now "start a session" decides all of these at once, and you can't touch them separately:

Straight answer, both halves.

## 1. Singleplayer

Four things stand in the way, and they are all small:

- `Store` builds its root as `path.join(repoPath, '.crew')` (`src/server/store.ts:39`). It cannot put history anywhere else.
- Hosting throws if the folder is not a git repo (`src/main/session.ts:253`).
- `git.start(AUTO_SYNC_MS)` runs unconditionally on both host and join (`src/main/session.ts:261`, `:299`).
- The server binds `0.0.0.0` (`src/server/index.ts:243`), though it already takes a `host` option.

The fix is to pass `Store` a root instead of making one, and to put a flag on `AppSession` that decides whether `GitSync` is constructed at all. Everything else hangs off `this.root`, so chat, docs, boards, attachments and music follow for free.

Local mode then means: root in app data, no `.crew` in the folder, no auto-commit, bind `127.0.0.1`. Push and Pull stay as the buttons they already are in `RepoControls`, since that is your code and not Crew's business. Drop the git check too, because `listRepoFiles` already walks the folder by hand when git fails and `GitSync.usable()` already no-ops.

One thing to get right up front: key the app data folder on the genesis commit (`git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD`), not a path hash. A path hash loses your history the day you move or reclone the folder. Fall back to a path hash when there is no git.

Multiplayer is untouched by any of this. The ws server hands every joiner a full snapshot on connect and broadcasts after that, and attachments and music go over http from the host. Git only moves code. So a local session is the same session with a different root and the sync loop not started, and turning sharing on later is one button that rebinds the socket.

## 2. Multiplayer without invite links

You need discovery, not a new transport. Two ways to get it with no server:

**Same network.** The host broadcasts a small UDP packet on a fixed port with its name, folder and ws address. `dgram` is in node, so no dependency. Home shows "on this network" and you click a row. That is the Discord feel, and it works whether or not the folder syncs, so it covers your work machine too if a coworker is on the same wifi.

**Same repo.** Write `.crew/host.json` with the current address as part of the sync pass. Anyone who pulls sees the session in their list without anyone sending anything. That is the repo being the server, and it costs one file. It only works for crews that already sync, so it is no help at work.

Run both and the list is just "places you can be right now", from either source. The `crew://` link stays as the fallback for the case neither covers, which is remote and not sharing a repo. That case genuinely needs a relay, and Tailscale is the way to have it without you running one.

+ import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'
+ import path from 'node:path'
+ import { runGit } from './git'
+ 
+ // Where a project's crew lives. In the folder is the shared one: chat, docs and
+ // boards ride in `.crew` and go out with the repo. On this machine is the same
+ // crew kept beside the app, so nothing is ever written into the project and git
+ // is never run.
+ export type CrewHome = 'folder' | 'private'
+ 
+ // A private crew is keyed on the repo's first commit rather than on where the
+ // folder happens to sit, so moving or recloning a project keeps its history. A
+ // folder with no commit yet has nothing to key on, so it takes a hash of its
+ // path and the key is remembered from then on.
+ export async function projectKey(folder: string): Promise<string> {
+   const result = await runGit(['rev-list', '--max-parents=0', 'HEAD'], folder)
+   const roots = result.code === 0 ? result.stdout.trim().split('\n') : []
+   const genesis = roots.map(line => line.trim()).filter(line => /^[0-9a-f]{40}$/.test(line)).at(-1)
+   if (genesis) return genesis.slice(0, 16)
+   return createHash('sha256').update(path.resolve(folder)).digest('hex').slice(0, 16)
+ }
+

I'm realizing there's an issue with how empty strings are handled in the key lookup logic. When `keyFor` returns an empty string for folder mode, that empty string gets stored, but then when checking `keyOf` later, the empty string isn't nullish so the fallback to `projectKey` doesn't trigger like it should.

The fix is to make `keyOf` return null for empty keys, so the conditional properly recomputes when needed. But actually, I'm thinking it's cleaner to just always compute a stable key for every project on first open, regardless of the home mode—that way switching between folder and private modes doesn't create these edge cases, and the remembered key is always meaningful.

I also notice `projectPlan` gets called in `startHost` when `opts.home` is undefined, which triggers another git check. I can inline that logic directly to avoid the duplicate execution. And there's a minor issue where `projectsDir()` throws if there's no projects path, but that's acceptable since the error surfaces in the UI anyway.

I'm noticing that Claude's parser is unique in never emitting errors, while Codex and Grok do. I need to check how Kimi handles errors in its implementation and tests. Looking at what Claude Code CLI actually outputs on failure, there are two message formats: one with `type: "result"` and `subtype: "error_during_execution"` when using `--output-format stream-json`, versus success messages that have `subtype: "success"` with the actual result payload.

Beyond those structured messages, startup failures print directly to stderr like "Invalid API key" or "Credit balance too low", which already get captured in `errText`. I'm thinking through whether to create a separate `failure.ts` file for handling exit reasons and error cleaning, or keep it in the existing cli.ts. A dedicated file makes sense since it's shared logic that deserves its own test coverage, and it aligns with keeping files focused and following DRY principles.

Now I'm mapping out the error messages for different signals and exit codes. SIGKILL and code 137 mean the system stopped Claude, likely due to memory. SIGTERM and 143 indicate it was stopped before completion. SIGINT and 130 mean it was interrupted. Crash signals like SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, and SIGABRT get their own message. For exit code 127, the command wasn't found. Code 126 means it's not executable. The tricky one is code 1 — it's generic, but when there's no output at all, it's usually an auth or startup issue with the Claude CLI. Rather than speculate, I should lean on whatever output the run actually produced. If the model generated text before failing, that text itself becomes the error message.

So the priority for failure messages should be: first check if the parser caught something specific, then look at stderr, then use any text the model produced before stopping (capped to keep it short), and finally fall back to exit-code descriptions. The key insight is that we're already discarding the run anyway, so recovering that partial text is better than losing it. But I need to be careful — a long partial answer could confuse things. The real fix is getting Claude's parser to report errors properly, and then the generic fallback just needs better exit-code and signal wording instead of "exited with code N".

I'm thinking about whether to include the model's last words as a safety net for CLIs whose parsers don't recognize their error format, like Kimi or Grok. The simplest approach is to skip that for now and focus on getting each model's parser to emit proper errors. I should add error parsing for Kimi too since it doesn't have any yet.

Now I'm considering what generic error shapes to handle across different models — things like `msg.error` as a string or object with a message field, `msg.type === 'error'`, or `role === 'error'`. For Claude specifically, I need to map the different terminal reasons and subtypes like `error_max_turns` or `error_during_execution` to user-friendly messages, and also check for the `is_api_error_message` flag at the assistant level.

I'm wondering whether error text should appear as a normal message step or if it gets handled differently — in the screenshot I saw only the red error line without a text bubble, which suggests the failed run might be replacing the steps rather than showing both. step.text:
Now I'm redesigning the Home page, which is the core piece. The main menu will display "Crew" as a large heading with a subtitle like "Pick up where you left off" or "Open a project to start," followed by a list showing recent projects with folder or desktop icons and their paths, plus recent joined sessions with globe or link icons showing the host and port information.

Below that are action buttons for opening a folder and joining with a link, with a footer row showing the user's avatar and name that can be clicked to change. I'm using ScreenSwap to manage navigation between different screens—places (the main list), name (for setting your name), home (for choosing where the project lives), and link (for pasting an invite)—each at different depth levels.

The tricky part is handling the initial flow when someone launches the app without a name set. I'm thinking the name screen should be the entry point, and after completing it you move deeper into the places list, so the animation reads naturally as progressing forward rather than backtracking.

For the actual interactions: picking a folder triggers a system dialog, and if it's a known project it opens immediately with remembered settings; if new, it goes to the home screen to let you choose where to work. Joining via an invite link requires passing a folder along with the link and name, since the runner needs a local directory to operate in—that's a constraint I need to work around in the flow.

Now I'm drafting the copy for the home screen. The title asks "Where should this crew live?" with two options: one to keep everything in the project folder so it syncs with git, another to keep it local to the machine with no git involvement. When a project isn't tracked, the first option's description changes to clarify that nothing syncs. The rows themselves become clickable actions rather than needing a separate button. I'm also adding a small close button on project rows so you can forget them.

For the visual markers, I'll use FolderGlyph to indicate folder-based homes and DesktopGlyph for private ones. I'm keeping `crew.name` and `crew.folder` in localStorage — the projects list handles most of the state, but these defaults are useful for the join screen. Next I'll write the Home component, using the existing `folderName` and `serverName` helpers. I'm also thinking through how transitions work between single-player and multiplayer modes — sharing a private project happens through the TopBar profile menu.

There's a wrinkle with joiners running GitSync unconditionally when they connect, which could be problematic for work repos, but that's out of scope for now. Changing a project's home location after creation would require moving files, so I'm skipping that and documenting the limitation. The component will follow the design system: rounded cards at 20px, pill-shaped buttons, ink and foreground scales, an Avatar primitive for the name row, and a tooltip on the forget button.

Writing the component now... Let me quickly check the Avatar and Tooltip signatures, plus look at Spinner and maybe reference an existing MenuItem-style row for the visual pattern.
Now the Home rebuild. Checking the primitives I'll use.

Fixed. The cause was on the Claude side of the parser.

**What was happening:** Claude exits 1 with **completely empty stderr** and writes the real reason into its JSON stream. `cli.ts` only looked at the parser's error and stderr, and the Claude parser never reported one, so every Claude failure fell through to the exit code. Verified live:

```
{"type":"result","is_error":true,"terminal_reason":"api_error","api_error_status":404,
 "result":"There's an issue with the selected model ... It may not exist or you may not have access to it."}
```

That message was sitting right there and being thrown away.

**What it does now**, against the real CLI:

```
Before: Claude exited with code 1
After:  There's an issue with the selected model (does-not-exist-9000).
        It may not exist or you may not have access to it. Run --model to pick a different model.
```

Four changes:

- `claude.ts` reads the reason out of a failed result: the message it carries, then the error, then plain words for `error_max_turns` and the rest. It keys on `is_error`, never the subtype, because the subtype still reads as `"success"` on an API error.
- An API error arrives as a message from the model wearing `is_api_error_message`. It is what went wrong rather than something the agent said, so it comes through as the reason instead of as a text bubble.
- `failure.ts` is the last resort, for a run that printed nothing anywhere. A signal or a known code goes into words ("could not be found on this machine", "was stopped by this machine, which usually means it ran out of memory") and only a genuine unknown says so, with the code in brackets. `cli.ts` was also dropping the signal, so anything the system killed used to read as "exited with code null".
- Stderr is cleaned before it becomes the message: colors stripped, the tail kept, so a stack trace does not land in the chat whole.

Kimi and Codex already put their errors on stderr or name them in the stream, so they were fine. The installer got the same wording treatment.

step.text:
RepoControls degrades gracefully when git isn't available, showing an unavailable status message and disabling itself. In private-home sessions on a git repo, `this.git` is null so it displays unavailable rather than tracked, which is a bit misleading since the project is actually tracked—Crew just isn't syncing it. Push and Pull buttons remain functional in private mode since they're user-controlled, not Crew's responsibility, though the automatic syncing won't happen.

The key insight is that `AppSession` should construct `GitSync` whenever the folder is tracked, but only start the auto-loop when home equals 'folder'. This gives you manual Push/Pull capability in private mode without auto-commit. I need to be careful with the `onBeforeRun` hook—in private mode it must not trigger a sync, and `session.onSyncNeeded` shouldn't schedule anything either. I'm restructuring `startHost` to conditionally set up the auto-sync loop and handlers based on whether we're in automatic mode, then I should verify that GitSync's constructor doesn't initialize any timers or writes on its own.
One more thing worth getting right: in local mode Push and Pull should still work by hand, just without the loop.

Part 1 is done and working. Here is what it is now.

## Starting

There is no host-or-join choice any more. You open a folder and you are in.

A project gets asked one question, the first time only: keep the crew **in the project** or **on this machine**. In the project is exactly what happens today, `.crew` in the folder, git loop running. On this machine puts the same `.crew` beside the app, so nothing is written into your work repo and nothing is ever committed by Crew. The answer is remembered per project, so it is never asked twice.

Two details that matter for your work case:

- Push and Pull still work in local mode. Git is there because it is your code and your button. Only the loop is off, so no auto-commit and no prompt waiting on a sync pass.
- The history is keyed on the repo's first commit, not the folder path, so moving or recloning the project keeps your chat. A folder with no git at all now opens too, instead of being refused.

## The main menu

Rebuilt. It is one list of places, newest first: every project you have opened and every crew you have joined, with the mark on the left saying where that project keeps its crew. Under it, the only two ways to reach a new one: open a folder, join with a link. The screens those lead to slide inside the same column through `ScreenSwap` rather than opening more boxes. Your name is asked once and then sits as a quiet row at the bottom.

## Going multiplayer

Nothing about the shared experience changed, because sharing is now just the listener moving. `setShared` closes the socket and reopens it on the same port bound to `0.0.0.0`. The session, its code, its history and everyone in it stay put; your own socket reconnects a second later on its own. It is one item in the profile menu, and turning it on copies the link in the same breath. A local session you share keeps its history in app data, and joiners still get the full snapshot, because multiplayer never needed git.

## Checked

`yarn tsc --noEmit` and `yarn build` clean. New suite `tests/local-session.integration.test.ts` (5 tests) covers no `.crew` in the folder, no commits, the genesis key surviving a move, the answer being remembered, an untracked folder opening, and sharing on and off mid-session without remaking it. `appsession`, `resume`, `saved-session`, `autosync` and `sync-guard` all pass. The tree did not typecheck when I started, from the earlier backend change landing without its tests; that is fixed.

Two things I did not do, both worth a decision:

- A joiner still runs the sync loop unconditionally in `startJoin`. Fine for a normal crew, wrong if you ever join a work session from a repo you cannot auto-commit.
- There is no way to move a project between the two homes after the fact. It means moving files, and I left it out rather than guess.

I found the issue — `ScreenSwap` in card mode uses `relative overflow-hidden` with a fixed height, and when the buttons inside `Places` scale up on hover with `hover:scale-[1.02]`, that 2% growth causes them to overflow and get clipped at the edges, which is why "Open a folder" and other elements are getting cut off on the left and right sides. The issue is likely the `hover:scale-[1.02]` combined with `overflow-hidden` — when the button scales up by about 3.8px on each side within the 384px container, those edges get clipped flat. For the TextField in screenshot 2, I should check if it has a similar focus ring or scale effect causing the right edge to cut off. The real fix would be to either remove the clipping in card mode since screens travel during animation, or add padding to the clipping box so the scaled content overshoots within that padded space instead of getting cut.

Actually, the cleaner approach: only clip while movement is happening. When at rest, let overflow be visible — that way the clipping only constrains content during the screen travel and height transitions, but releases once everything settles. I'd track a `moving` state that activates when the screen changes or height transitions, then clears after the animation completes.

Now I need to check if overflow-hidden is being applied elsewhere too — Jamel mentioned it's happening across the experience, so I should search for places where it's combined with scale hovers to see the broader pattern.

step.text:
Jamel wants a much more elaborate boot background—something visually striking like a starfield racing at lightspeed with the mark landing in it, inspired by Star Wars. This is a significant upgrade from the current soft glow aesthetic. I'm thinking about how to approach this since the codebase already has shader infrastructure from the music cover system and canvas painting in the games, so there's a foundation to build on.

The concept is the crew arriving out of lightspeed: stars streak toward the viewer in 3D perspective, then decelerate as the mark lands and drops out of warp. The mark's discs arrive with the light running across them, matching the existing crew-join animation. For implementation, a 2D canvas approach would be efficient and straightforward—tracking N stars with depth coordinates, projecting them to screen space each frame with perspective, and drawing streaks that ease from fast to slow as the animation progresses.

For the color palette, I'm keeping the crew in black and white while the mark uses its sanctioned mesh color, with white stars that bleed into the mesh colors near the center. The glow behind the mark provides the color accent while maintaining a clean, honest palette.

I'm organizing this as `src/renderer/src/media/warp.ts` to handle the warp logic and drawing separately from the React component, following the project's pattern with `paint.ts` for games and `coverArt.ts` for media. The module will export types and functions for creating stars, stepping the animation forward each frame, and painting the warp effect to the canvas.

Now I'm thinking through the timing: the warp starts at full lightspeed with long streaks, decelerates around 700ms, then by 1000ms the stars become points drifting slowly as the mark's discs arrive. The glow blooms and everything lifts away. I need to restructure Boot into three phases—the warp running alone, then the mark arriving as the warp slows, then the final lift-off—so the crew-join animation triggers when the mark actually appears.

For the timings, I'm aiming for the warp to run at full speed for 450ms, decelerate over the next 450ms, and have the mark mount around 700ms as that deceleration finishes, landing by about 1420ms total. That puts the whole boot sequence around 1500ms, which is longer than Arc's 1.2s but acceptable for a launch moment. I'm considering whether the mark's arrival should actually be the deceleration itself—the stars slowing down as the discs arrive, with the flash across the mark marking that moment of impact.

I'm refining the timing so the warp holds at full speed for 600ms, the mark mounts at that point, and the star speed eases down between 600 and 1350ms, with the whole sequence landing by 1500ms. The existing crew flash should align nicely with this deceleration phase. I also want to add a radial vignette to darken the edges and focus attention on the center, plus have the stars streak toward the viewer from a center vanishing point. Still deciding whether to keep the glow effect.

Now I'm thinking about the implementation structure: I'll create a `warp.ts` file with pure math and rendering logic that's testable, and a `Warp.tsx` component that handles the canvas setup and animation loop. The canvas needs to account for device pixel ratio for performance. I should also write tests to verify the star behavior—that they move toward the viewer and wrap correctly when they pass the camera.
Jamel wants much more. Let me check the existing canvas idioms before writing it.

step.text:
I can reuse `useGameLoop` for this. I'm splitting the warp effect into three files: one for the math—calculating star positions in 3D space, the projection, and the speed curve—another for rendering, and a React component to tie it together with the canvas and animation loop. Then I'll wire it all into `Boot.tsx`.

Actually, let me reorganize: I'll put the warp pieces under `src/renderer/src/components/boot/` to mirror the structure of `components/game/` and `components/music/`, with `views/Boot.tsx` composing them together.

For the warp itself, each star has x and y coordinates in a square around the origin and a z depth. As the star moves toward the camera, I project it onto the screen using perspective math, and when it gets too close, I respawn it at the far plane with new coordinates. The streak effect comes from drawing a line between where the star was and where it is now, creating that lightspeed look. I'll brighten stars as they approach and make the lines thicker closer to the viewer, fading them out as they recede.

For the speed curve, I want the warp to hold at maximum speed for a moment, then decelerate smoothly down to a drift speed using an easing function. The dramatic feel comes from a brief acceleration into the jump followed by a hard deceleration—like ships in Star Wars stretching the stars as they jump to lightspeed, then settling back down.

For the visual, I'll use white stars with some picking up subtle tints from the mark's own colors, so it feels like the light from the mark is scattered through the field. The mesh glow near the center will bleed into the surrounding stars, creating that cohesive arrival moment.

I want to add a vignette — a radial gradient that darkens the edges and keeps focus on the mark itself. A gentle roll during the fast phase could add depth without overcomplicating things, so I'll keep it subtle and let it decay as the speed decreases. For reduced motion, I'll just show the mark without the warp effect.

Now I need to set up the files and export the blob colors from CrewMark so I can use them for the star tints.

Defining the warp module constants... Writing star generation logic... Writing projection logic... I'll clear the canvas each frame with `clearRect` to keep it transparent and let the background show through, though a subtle persistence layer with low-alpha fills could add motion blur—but that's complex over transparency, so the long streaks alone should sell the speed. To make this feel richer than a plain starfield, I'm adding soft nebula gradients in the mesh colors drifting slowly behind the stars for depth, and tinting individual stars to tie them to the mark's palette.

Actually, I realize `CrewGlow` (the blurred mesh bloom) already serves as the nebula when the mark lands, so I can layer it nicely: canvas warp with stars and vignette in back, the bloom effect as the mark touches down, then the mark itself on top. I'll add a couple of slow-moving nebula blobs sourced from the same mesh colors at very low alpha so the field feels alive rather than just black space.

I need to verify that reusing `useGameLoop` from the boot component is the right call here—it's DRY but the naming might be misleading.

Writing the files now:

1. `src/renderer/src/components/boot/warp.ts` — numbers
2. `src/renderer/src/components/boot/drawWarp.ts` — paint
3. `src/renderer/src/components/boot/Warp.tsx` — canvas + loop
4.

Now I need to export the mesh colors from CrewMark so I can use them for tinting the warp stars. I'll grab those colors and use them selectively — mostly white stars with occasional tinted ones based on a random threshold. The color logic belongs in the draw function since it's a rendering concern, so I'll define how each star picks its color there based on its tint value.
Now the real thing: the crew drops out of lightspeed. First the numbers, on their own.

+ // The field the app opens on, as numbers. Nothing here draws anything or knows
+ // what a canvas is, the way a game's rules stand apart from its picture.
+ export type Star = { x: number; y: number; z: number; tint: number }
+ 
+ export type View = { width: number; height: number; reach: number }
+ 
+ // Where the far plane is, and how close a star gets before it is behind you.
+ export const DEPTH = 1
+ export const NEAR = 0.055
+ 
+ // Lightspeed, and the drift it settles into once the crew has arrived.
+ export const LIGHT = 2.1
+ export const DRIFT = 0.03
+ 
+ // How long the field holds at speed before it drops out of it, and how long the
+ // drop takes. The mark lands on the end of that, so the two are one movement.
+ export const HOLD = 0.38
+ export const SETTLE = 1.15
+ 
+ // How far behind itself a star is smeared. One frame's travel is a few pixels
+ // and reads as a dot however fast the field is going, so the trail is stretched
+ // past it: that stretch is the whole of what makes speed look like speed.
+ export const TRAIL = 3.4
+ 
+ export function warpSpeed(t: number): number {
+   if (t <= HOLD) return LIGHT
+   const u = Math.min((t - HOLD) / SETTLE, 1)
+   return LIGHT + (DRIFT - LIGHT) * (1 - Math.pow(1 - u, 3))
+ }
+ 
+ // A star stands somewhere on a disc facing the viewer, and the disc is wider
+ // than the window, so the corners are as full as the middle.
+ function spawn(random: () => number, z: number): Star {
+   const angle = random() * Math.PI * 2
+   const reach = Math.sqrt(random())
+   return { x: Math.cos(angle) * reach, y: Math.sin(angle) * reach, z, tint: random() }
+ }
+ 
+ export function makeStars(count: number, random: () => number): Star[] {
+   const stars: Star[] = []
+   for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) stars.push(spawn(random, NEAR + random() * (DEPTH - NEAR)))
+   return stars
+ }
+ 
+ // One frame of travel. A star that has gone past comes back at the far plane,
+ // so the field never runs out however long the window is left open.
+ export function stepStars(stars: Star[], speed: number, dt: number, random: () => number): void {
+   for (let i = 0; i < stars.length; i += 1) {
+     const star = stars[i]
+     star.z -= speed * dt
+     if (star.z <= NEAR) stars[i] = spawn(random, DEPTH)
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ export function viewOf(width: number, height: number): View {
+   return { width, height, reach: Math.min(width, height) * 0.11 }
+ }
+ 
+ export function project(x: number, y: number, z: number, view: View): { x: number; y: number } {
+   return { x: view.width / 2 + (x / z) * view.reach, y: view.height / 2 + (y / z) * view.reach }
+ }
+ 
+ // A star arrives out of the dark rather than switching on, and it is brightest
+ // once it is near. Both ends matter: without the first the far plane is a wall
+ // of dots blinking into being, and everything is the same star without the
+ // second.
+ export function brightness(z: number): number {
+   const arriving = Math.min((DEPTH - z) / 0.3, 1)
+   const near = 0.35 + 0.65 * (1 - z / DEPTH)
+   return Math.max(0, arriving) * near
+ }
+

+ import { MESH_COLORS } from '../CrewMark'
+ import { DEPTH, TRAIL, brightness, project, type Star, type View } from './warp'
+ 
+ // Most of the field is white, and a few of them carry the light the mark is
+ // made of, so the color in the picture comes from one table rather than from a
+ // palette the boot made up for itself.
+ const TINTED = 0.22
+ 
+ const CLOUDS = [
+   { color: MESH_COLORS[0], x: 0.3, y: 0.36, r: 0.62, alpha: 0.2, drift: 0.055, lag: 0 },
+   { color: MESH_COLORS[1], x: 0.66, y: 0.6, r: 0.7, alpha: 0.17, drift: -0.04, lag: 1.9 },
+   { color: MESH_COLORS[3], x: 0.78, y: 0.3, r: 0.5, alpha: 0.13, drift: 0.07, lag: 3.4 }
+ ]
+ 
+ function starColor(star: Star): string {
+   if (star.tint > TINTED) return '#ffffff'
+   return MESH_COLORS[Math.floor((star.tint / TINTED) * MESH_COLORS.length) % MESH_COLORS.length]
+ }
+ 
+ // The dust the field is travelling through. It is drawn behind everything and
+ // moves at a fraction of the stars, which is what gives the flight a far
+ // distance as well as a near one.
+ function paintClouds(ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, view: View, t: number, lit: number): void {
+   ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'lighter'
+   for (const cloud of CLOUDS) {
+     const swing = Math.sin(t * cloud.drift * Math.PI * 2 + cloud.lag)
+     const cx = (cloud.x + swing * 0.05) * view.width
+     const cy = (cloud.y + Math.cos(t * cloud.drift * Math.PI * 2 + cloud.lag) * 0.04) * view.height
+     const r = cloud.r * Math.min(view.width, view.height)
+     const wash = ctx.createRadialGradient(cx, cy, 0, cx, cy, r)
+     wash.addColorStop(0, cloud.color)
+     wash.addColorStop(1, 'transparent')
+     ctx.globalAlpha = cloud.alpha * lit
+     ctx.fillStyle = wash
+     ctx.fillRect(0, 0, view.width, view.height)
+   }
+   ctx.globalAlpha = 1
+   ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'source-over'
+ }
+ 
+ // A star is a line from where it was to where it is. At speed that line crosses
+ // the window, and as the field slows the two ends close up until what is left
+ // is a point, which is the whole of dropping out of lightspeed.
+ function paintStars(
+   ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
+   stars: Star[],
+   view: View,
+   speed: number,
+   dt: number
+ ): void {
+   ctx.lineCap = 'round'
+   ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'lighter'
+   const smear = speed * dt * TRAIL
+   for (const star of stars) {
+     const now = project(star.x, star.y, star.z, view)
+     if (now.x < -80 || now.x > view.width + 80 || now.y < -80 || now.y > view.height + 80) continue
+     const was = project(star.x, star.y, Math.min(star.z + smear, DEPTH), view)
+     const lit = brightness(star.z)
+     ctx.globalAlpha = Math.min(lit, 1)
+     ctx.strokeStyle = starColor(star)
+     ctx.lineWidth = Math.max(0.7, 2.4 * (1 - star.z / DEPTH))
+     ctx.beginPath()
+     ctx.moveTo(was.x, was.y)
+     ctx.lineTo(now.x, now.y)
+     ctx.stroke()
+   }
+   ctx.globalAlpha = 1
+   ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'source-over'
+ }
+ 
+ // The edges go down so the middle is the only place to look, which is where the
+ // mark lands.
+ function paintVignette(ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, view: View): void {
+   const half = Math.max(view.width, view.height) * 0.72
+   const shade = ctx.createRadialGradient(
+     view.width / 2,
+     view.height / 2,
+     half * 0.3,
+     view.width / 2,
+     view.height / 2,
+     half
+   )
+   shade.addColorStop(0, 'rgba(0,0,0,0)')
+   shade.addColorStop(1, 'rgba(0,0,0,0.72)')
+   ctx.fillStyle = shade
+   ctx.fillRect(0, 0, view.width, view.height)
+ }
+ 
+ export function paintWarp(
+   ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D,
+   stars: Star[],
+   view: View,
+   speed: number,
+   dt: number,
+   t: number
+ ): void {
+   ctx.clearRect(0, 0, view.width, view.height)
+   paintClouds(ctx, view, t, Math.min(t / 1.2, 1))
+   paintStars(ctx, stars, view, speed, dt)
+   paintVignette(ctx, view)
+ }
+

+ import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react'
+ import useGameLoop from '../game/useGameLoop'
+ import { paintWarp } from './drawWarp'
+ import { makeStars, stepStars, viewOf, warpSpeed, type Star } from './warp'
+ 
+ const STARS = 460
+ 
+ // The flight the app opens on. It is drawn straight onto the canvas every
+ // frame, never held in state, the way the music's bars are: a render a frame
+ // would cost more than the picture is worth.
+ export default function Warp({ still }: { still: boolean }) {
+   const canvas = useRef<HTMLCanvasElement>(null)
+   const stars = useRef<Star[]>([])
+   const age = useRef(0)
+ 
+   useEffect(() => {
+     stars.current = makeStars(STARS, Math.random)
+   }, [])
+ 
+   useEffect(() => {
+     const el = canvas.current
+     if (!el) return
+     const size = () => {
+       const ratio = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2)
+       el.width = Math.round(el.clientWidth * ratio)
+       el.height = Math.round(el.clientHeight * ratio)
+       el.getContext('2d')?.setTransform(ratio, 0, 0, ratio, 0, 0)
+     }
+     size()
+     const watching = new ResizeObserver(size)
+     watching.observe(el)
+     return () => watching.disconnect()
+   }, [])
+ 
+   useGameLoop(dt => {
+     const el = canvas.current
+     const ctx = el?.getContext('2d')
+     if (!el || !ctx) return
+     age.current += dt
+     const speed = warpSpeed(age.current)
+     stepStars(stars.current, speed, dt, Math.random)
+     paintWarp(ctx, stars.current, viewOf(el.clientWidth, el.clientHeight), speed, dt, age.current)
+   }, !still)
+ 
+   return <canvas ref={canvas} aria-hidden className="absolute inset-0 w-full h-full" />
+ }
+

+ // A field that has to look the same on every machine is stepped by hand here,
+ // so nothing about it is left to whatever a frame happened to take.
+ function steady(seed: number): () => number {
+   let at = seed
+   return () => {
+     at = (at * 1664525 + 1013904223) % 4294967296
+     return at / 4294967296
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ describe('the field the app opens on', () => {
+   it('opens at lightspeed and settles into a drift', () => {
+     expect(warpSpeed(0)).toBe(LIGHT)
+     expect(warpSpeed(HOLD)).toBe(LIGHT)
+     expect(warpSpeed(HOLD + SETTLE)).toBeCloseTo(DRIFT, 6)
+     expect(warpSpeed(HOLD + SETTLE + 10)).toBeCloseTo(DRIFT, 6)
+   })
+ 
+   it('only ever slows down', () => {
+     let last = Infinity
+     for (let t = 0; t < 3; t += 0.02) {
+       const speed = warpSpeed(t)
+       expect(speed).toBeLessThanOrEqual(last + 1e-9)
+       last = speed
+     }
+   })
+ 
+   it('stands every star in front of the viewer and inside the field', () => {
+     const stars = makeStars(500, steady(7))
+     expect(stars).toHaveLength(500)
+     for (const star of stars) {
